MR. LACOMBE-TRANSLATION OF REMARKS IN DEBATE ON JUNE 25
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to a questioa of privilege. Last Wednesday I withdrew unconditionally a statement which I had made in French in this house on June 25. Now, using my privilege as a member of parliament, I should like to ask the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to be just and fair to me. Speaking in this house on June 28 the Prime Minister quoted from the English debates of June 25 last. This citation was as follows:
We have here in the cabinet three new millionaires who have made their money since the war's outbreak. We shall denounce them at the proper time and place. Fortunes are being built up.
That citation is reported at page 4072 of the English Debates of June 28, 1943. This is an absolutely false translation of a part of my speech delivered in French on June 25. Consequently I should like to ask the right hon. the Prime Minister to withdraw this citation or to give instructions to the translator to correct this translation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MR. LACOMBE-TRANSLATION OF REMARKS IN DEBATE ON JUNE 25

I am sure the house would wish me to be absolutely fair with the hon. gentleman, and no one is more anxious to be so than myself. I would remind him that the citation which I used on Wednesday was the citation as it appears in Hansard in French and I used only that citation and had reference to no other in the remarks I made. It was pointed out at the time that the French translation, in the mind of the hon. member who has just spoken, and I think I may say in the minds also of many other hon. members, was not a correct translation. But that was in no sense my fault or the fault of the government; it is a matter which concerns the translation staff of the house. I would say for that reason
I think my hon. friend, in desiring to have any correction made, so far as Hansard is concerned, should address the Speaker of the house rather than myself. He will find His Honour the Speaker quite ready, I am sure, to see that an accurate translation is given. If he adopts that procedure he will find, I am sure, on the part of all there will be every disposition to see that a proper translation is substituted for the one that appears in Hansard.

maintopic: MR. GRAYDON-REFERENCE TO EDITORIAL IN THE ' TORONTO "GLOBE AND MAH,"

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: MR. GRAYDON-REFERENCE TO EDITORIAL IN THE ' TORONTO "GLOBE AND MAH,"
speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege based upon an editorial appearing in to-day's issue of the Toronto Globe and Mail, which reflects upon His Majesty's Loyal Opposition and myself as leader. The editorial, among other things, says that:
Last week Doctor W. J. Edmonston Scott, M.A., who served at Ottawa as a censor in languages of central and western Europe from 1939 to 1943, supplied in a letter published in this newspaper definite confirmation of the validity of its charges about the government's scandalously inquisitorial abuse of the powers of censorship conferred upon it by the War Measures Act. Doctor Scott did not merely give general support to our allegations, but he rovided very damning evidence to justify them y quoting a special memorandum, dated May 1, 1942, which was issued to examiners, and ran as follows:
"All letters observed in the mails containing information regarding women's political activities in all parts of the world and women's activities in connection with post-war reconstruction should be specially submitted to this office and the file reference C.11292-38 quoted."
No denial has been made of this allegation of Doctor Scott, and presumably no denial is possible. It is so disturbing that even a staunch supporter of the government like the Winnipeg Free Press has been moved to describe it as a gross abuse of the powers of censorship, upon which the fullest possible light should be directed, and to demand that the Minister of National War Services, who is responsible for the censorship, should be cross-examined in great detail about the scope of its operations.
If a parliamentary opposition has one duty more compelling than another, it is to act as a vigilant watchdog against all unwarranted governmental assaults upon fundamental principles of liberty. But, so far, from the opposition benches not even a whisper of protest has been heard against this proved assault. All the opposition groups have a measure of culpability in the matter, as any of their members could have raised the issue. But a special degree of blame for a deplorable laxity must attach to Mr. Graydon, because the leader of the official opposition has by tradition a special responsibility for bringing a government to book for such arrogant abuse of its powers as has been revealed, especially when they strike at the roots of personal liberties. He should have lost no time in proceeding to cross-examine the Minister of National War Services about this matter.

I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the editorial in question is evidently based upon a misunderstanding of the position of the opposition and myself in this matter, and I desire to deny the charge that we have been in any way remiss in our duties .with respect to the issue in question.
On Wednesday last, after consultation with me, the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) took the necessary steps to ask for the production of a copy of all censorship orders, regulations or instructions issued under government authority since the outbreak of war. This appears in Votes and Proceedings of Thursday, July 1. The hon. member's motion was prompted largely by our desire to have a proper basis for examination of the ministry with respect to the allegations raised by Doctor Scott and certain newspapers, particularly the Winnipeg Free Press and the Toronto (Globe and Mail. We felt that a fuller and more complete examination of censorship matters generally and this case in particular could best be accomplished when the papers asked for had been tabled and a more appropriate opportunity presented itself for careful and detailed examination of the ministry. I rise therefore on this question of privilege to put the record straight so far as our position as an opposition is concerned.

subtopic: MESSAGES OF GREETING AND GOOD WISHES FROM REPRESENTATIVES OF OTHER COUNTRIES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MESSAGES OF GREETING AND GOOD WISHES FROM REPRESENTATIVES OF OTHER COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel that hon. members of the house will be pleased to know that yesterday, Dominion day, I received on behalf of their governments, either by letter or by personal call, greetings to Canada, good wishes and many expressions of thanks from members of the foreign diplomatic service resident in Ottawa at this time. There were also a number of telegrams received from different countries, some of which I have felt would be of special interest to the house, and which the house might wish to have as a matter of record on Hansard. It will not take more than a minute or two for me to refer to them; they illustrate the appreciation felt by other countries of Canada's present position and of the assistance received from Canada during the period of the war.
One message directed to His Excellency the Governor General was from King Peter of Yugoslavia, who it will be remembered visited Ottawa not so very long ago. The message was as follows:
On the occasion of the national day of Canada I offer Your Excellency my warmest greetings and best wishes for the welfare and prosperity of the dominion and of the gallant Canadian people.
From the Yugoslav Minister for Foreign Affairs in London, a message was addressed to myself in the following words:
I avail myself of the Canadian Dominion Day to convey to you my warmest greetings and heartfelt good wishes for the happiness and prosperity of your great nation.
A message addressed to myself as Prime Minister came from General Sikorski, Prime Minister of Poland, who is at the present time in Cairo. General Sikorski, it will be recalled, has visited Canada on two or three occasions in the course of the war:
On the occasion of your national holiday I send you and the gallant Canadian nation my heartiest congratulations, best wishes, all success. May I assure you the Polish nation and myself greatly admire Canada's magnificent contribution to the allies' cause on the battlefields of this war. By the same opportunity please accept my personal best greetings.
A communication came also from the Polish government in London, through the Deputy Prime Minister, Mr. Stanislaw Mikolajezyk, which reads:
On the occasion of Canada's day please accept, Mr. Prime Minister, the cordial greetings and heartfelt wishes of the government and people of Poland. We shall always remember with
72537-271i
gratitude the support which your great country is so generously giving us in the hour of need. I am sure that the bonds of friendship forged during the years of our common struggle will continue after victory is achieved and contribute to the building up of a new international community.
His Excellency the President of China, Lin Sen, sent the following message to His Excellency the Governor General:
On the occasion of Dominion day, I have great pleasure in extending to you on behalf of the national government and people of China my hearty felicitations and best wishes for your personal welfare and the prosperity of Canada.
The following message was also received from Chungking, addressed to myself as Prime Minister, from Premier and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek:
On the occasion of your Dominion day I have great pleasure to extend to you my hearty felicitations. I believe that our traditional friendship which has been enhanced by comradeship in arms not only strengthens our united war effort to crush our common enemy but will stand us in good stead in our post-war cooperation to establish an enduring peace. May. I also take this opportunity to express to you my personal thanks for the kind hospitality which your government and the Canadian people extended to my wife during her recent stay in your country and my best wishes for your health and the happiness of the Canadian people.
There were three or four important messages from south American countries. From the Argentine republic a communication from the Hon. Segundo R. Stomi, Minister of Foreign Affairs, as follows:
It is with special pleasure that I address myself to you, the Prime Minister, to reaffirm, on the occasion of the commemoration of Dominion day the deep friendship of the government and people of my country for the government and people of Canada. The Argentine republic, linked to Canada by reason of our dwelling in the same hemisphere and by common ideals of progress, wishes to expand and consolidate the friendly relations which unite both countries.
The following message was received from the President of the Republic of Brazil, His Excellency Doctor Getrilo Vargas. It was communicated through the Minister, Doctor de Millo Franco:
The President of the republic of the United States of Brazil has instructed me by telegram to convey to you and to the Canadian people his heartiest congratulations and those of the Brazilian people on the occasion of the celebration of Dominion day. The Minister for Foreign Affairs of Brazil, Doctor Oswaldo Aranha, also instructed me to congratulte you on his behalf, which I also do in my own name.
It is with great pleasure that I give course to said instructions. The commemoration of Dominion day cannot be considered by the nations of the Americas only as the celebration of a great Canadian date, but as that of a great American date, as it represents the birth of one more sister nation.
Canadian Navy

In only seventy-six years Canada has raised herself to the outstanding position she occupies to-day in the concert of nations; it is a miracle accomplished by her great people and by her leaders, and I can assure you that we Brazilians look to her with the proud admiration that a member of a same family has for the successes of another member.
The President of Brazil also sent the following message to His Excellency the Governor General:
On the seventy-sixth anniversary of the dominion I beg Your Excellency to accept my warmest wishes for the ever-increasing pros-.perity of Canada and for the personal welfare of Your Excellency.
A message also came from the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Chile, Mr. Joaquin Fernandez, as follows;
In the name of the government of Chile it affords me pleasure to greet you and the Canadian people on the occasion of the anniversary of confederation and to express our best wishes for the happiness of your government and yourself.
A message as follows was received also from the Vice-President of the Republic of Uruguay, His Excellency Alberto Guani, who recently visited Canada:
I congratulate you very cordially seeing in your people and in yourself staunch and distinguished supporters of right and liberty in this hour of spiritual trial for all humanity. I renew my gratitude for the amicable welcome extended recently in your admirable country.
As I have already said, other countries having legations in Ottawa sent messages of friendliest greetings either conveyed by letter or expressed in person by their ministers.

subtopic: PROPORTION OF HIGH RANKING OFFICERS AS COMPARED WITH OTHER NAVIES

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): Last week the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) asked a question regarding the number of high-ranking officers in the Canadian navy, and if I am in order I should like to reply now. I am sorry that last week I gave the figure of seven as the number of those in the Canadian navy holding the rank of commodore or higher. The correct number is eight, but I was speaking from memory at the time and I had forgotten that quite recently another commodore was appointed. The total number, then, in the Canadian navy holding the rank of commodore and higher is eight, ahd a comparison with other navies, for which the hon. member asked as well, would run approximately as follows. The figures are not

perhaps entirely exact, because it is difficult to ascertain the precise strength of other navies, but I think they are substantially correct.
In the United Kingdom there is one officer of the rank of commodore and above for every 3,000 men. In Australia there is one officer of that rank for every 5,200 men. In the United States there is one officer of that rank for every 5,500 men, and in Canada one officer of that rank for every 7,500 men. It will be seen, therefore, that the reports which the hon. gentleman received to the effect that we had a great many high-ranking officers in the Canadian navy, as compared to other navies, are not correct, but that, on the contrary, we have many less of such high-ranking officers, proportionately, than any of the other navies to which I have referred.

subtopic: CANCELLATION OF CONTRACT FOR BUILDING OF TUGS AT PICTOU, N.S.-REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CANCELLATION OF CONTRACT FOR BUILDING OF TUGS AT PICTOU, N.S.-REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION
speechtext: I should like to ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply if he has been able to reconsider the cancellation of the contract for building two tugs, which was given some time ago to Ferguson Brothers in Pictou. It has been represented to me that the minister does not understand the situation in that yard. This company took on the contract in good faith; about thirty per cent of the preliminary work has been done; it has been financed entirely by the company; this concern has about a thousand men in its different undertakings, and has not encroached in the slightest degree on the operations of the other shipbuilding yards in Pictou. They feel that if they were allowed to complete their contract, as they are prepared to do, it would form the basis of a post-war industry, of which we have very few in Nova Scotia. I should like to ask the minister if he has been able to reconsider, and reconsider favourably, representations made to him by the company and by the people of Pictou and, I believe, by the government of Nova Scotia.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
subtopic: CANCELLATION OF CONTRACT FOR BUILDING OF TUGS AT PICTOU, N.S.-REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION
speechtext:
The Ferguson yard at Pictou
has been enlarged to provide facilities for the repair of naval and merchant vessels. A number of other yards have also been expanded for that purpose. The question arises as to whether the facilities can be utilized for other purposes, when there is an urgent need for repair facilities. At the

Munitions and Supply-Tugs
moment the full facilities of the Ferguson yard are required and are being used for the repair of ships.
I	may say that the understanding I have from my officers 'with respect to the tug situation is that it was felt that a steel company at Trenton had facilities for building tugs. May I add that tugs of the size we are discussing do not require to be built in a modern shipyard. They usually are built at a number of places along the great lakes and in the St. Lawrence, that are not by any stretch of the imagination shipyards. They are very simple to build, and they cost about $400,000 each.
Arrangements were made to build two of these tugs at Trenton. A dispute about wages arose, as to whether the tugs should be built on shipyard wages or steel plant wages, and the Trenton plant decided it did not want the tugs built there. Without the knowledge Of the department the tugs were moved into the shipyard that had been reserved for repair purposes, or enlarged for repair purposes, at Pictou. The net result of that would be that facilities reserved for repair purposes could be used to build tugs, or for work other than repairs. The whole principle was being established that yards which had been designated to repair ships had the privilege of taking any contracts they liked, and doing it in repair yards. The result was that the contract for two tugs was cancelled, by arrangement with the Ferguson company. Arrangements were made in my office some six weeks ago-

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN PLACEMENT OP CARS
speechtext: Would the Minister of Agriculture throw a little light on this question of alcohol from wheat? A statement was made in the house by the Minister of Munitions and Supply that in the manufacture of alcohol from wheat returns to farmers would be around only 25 to 35 cents a bushel. On the other hand, Doctor Archibald, speaking to the committee on agriculture yesterday, said that if alcohol were made from wheat, given a wheat yield of twenty bushels to the acre, the farmer would get a return of $17 an acre, which works out to 85 cents a bushel. That is different from the figure given by the Minister of Munitions and Supply; I suggest there must be some explanation, fo the difference between 25 or 30 cents on the one hand and 85' cents on the other. Will the minister give the committee some information on this point?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN PLACEMENT OP CARS
speechtext:
Of course one would require to have the figures used by both the parties referred to, and also the basis for those figures, before he could explain the difference between them. The difference which might be there is probably based upon the facts that are usually run into when you are discussing costs of productions or returns per acre. The statement made to the committee ,by Doctor Archibald, which I happen to have in my hand, contains the estimated value of various crops as sources of alcohol. Wheat is taken at twenty bushels to the acre, and the production of alcohol is stated to be

4-24 gallons per hundred pounds. Taking that as a basis it goes on to say that the total value of the crop per acre is $17.51. I am not certain what figures were used by those who worked out the cost for the Minister of Munitions and Supply, but in all probability the average production and the average cost were taken into consideration. The only statement with regard to the matter that I would care to make at the present time is that all the information I have seen, all the figures that have been compiled, indicate that wheat would have to be produced at a much lower cost than that at which I think any farmer in western Canada would be prepared to produce it, in order to.permit the production of alcohol at a cost comparable with the cost of production from other sources.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN PLACEMENT OP CARS
speechtext:
I should like to direct the attention of the minister to an article appearing in Business Week of June 12, 1943. I quote from pages 72 and 75 as follows:
The chemurgist's diream of grain alcohol as the answer to farm surpluses may yet come true -and with it a lengthening horizon of post-war possibilities for the rubber, oil, and chemical industries-through a process of protein extraction which promises to make alcohol a cheap by-product.
And again:
The process was discovered less than four months ago by Irvin W. Tucker, a young chemist in the department of agriculture working under direction of Doctor A. K. Balls, chief of the department's enzyme research laboratory. Park and Tilfordi developed it commercially.
The article goes into>
further details and concludes as follows:
Heretofore, chemurgists who grappled with the question of farm surpluses habitually stubbed their toes on two hard problems: there was no market for the tremendous volume of alcohol that could be produced from farm products, and the cost of farm alcohol was prohibitively high. The war has solved the first problem. . . . Balls and Tucker appear to have solved the second.
This article would seem to suggest that a process has been discovered which considerably reduces the cost of making alcohol from grain, a matter which is of prime importance to Canada. I should like to know whether there is contact between the Department of Agriculture and research such as is here indicated.
I should also like to draw the attention of the minister to an article which appeared in the June, 1943, issue of the Reader's Digest. This is a condensation from the Christian Science Monitor. I quote from pages 81, 82 and S3 as follows:
At Institute, West Virginia, a superb plant 77 acres in area is turning out rubber at the rate of 90,000 long tons a year. That is almost

Supply-Agriculture
one-sixth as much as we used to need in normal times-and as much as 100,000 Malay natives gather from 18,000,000 rubber trees.
The writer of this article would seem to hold no brief for grain or petroleum; but note what he says:
The process used at Institute happens to make its butadiene out of alcohol. The alcohol now comes from corn.
I am emphasizing two points. First, there does seem to be a considerable volume of synthetic rubber being manufactured in the United States from alcohol produced from grain. Second, there would appear to have been recent discoveries which reduce the cost of this process.

speechtext: Did Doctor Archibald give the figures at which alcohol would have to be sold in order to bring that return?

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN PLACEMENT OP CARS
speechtext: I have in my hand the document which was before the committee this morning when Doctor Archibald was giving his evidence. This is a survey of Canadian research on the utilization of farm products by the chemurgie committee of the Canadian chamber of commerce. It will be recalled by those who were present at the committee this morning that Doctor Archibald referred to certain reports that had been made, I think by Doctor Speakman. This document is the last word on the matter in so far as Canada is concerned. Figures are given based on cost according to United States practice and according to European practice. According to United States practice, with wheat at 60 cents the cost would be 53-4 cents for the alcohol at the plant. According to the European process, with wheat at 60 cents the cost of alcohol would be 39-6 cents at the plant. As I indicated at the beginning, after examining the figures which had been secured in the United States up to that time, as well as the experiences on the European continent, it appeared that even with wheat at 60 cents, the cost of alcohol would be 53-4 cents under the American practice and 39-6 cents under the European.

It is with some hesitation that I rise to speak on this matter, because I appreciate that in time of war it is not the popular thing to try to divert public thinking from the immediate necessities of war and the problems which they have created. But, having listened in at some of the conferences of the Empire Parliamentary Association and tried to look into the future, it seems to me that, in view of the adjustments which are being made by other countries, allied and anti-ally, western Canadian agriculture is likely to be faced with a serious problem so far as markets are concerned for what are now the natural products of the prairies.
IMr. Slaght.j
It is not unknown that since the war began the British isles have increased their agricultural production from thirty-five per cent of their national needs to, now, seventy per cent of their national needs. What effect is that going to have on the potential post-war market for the great bulk of, shall we say, western Canada's agricultural production? Is it not a moot question whether Canada can hold the favourable position she now has so far as the British market is concerned? And if peradven-ture the European countries which during the war have increased1 their agricultural production should be inclined to continue to do so, what then? They have done this through force of necessity, taking advantage of scientific research and mass production methods; and I am greatly exercised and concerned as to what we in Canada-I am not selfish in this respect, because what applies to western Canada applies also to eastern Canada-are to do with our surplus agricultural products if we continue to produce wheat and as we have done during the war. It may be that we shall have to change, if not our methods, the products of our farms in the west. The war has taught the people of Alberta, at any rate, how to raise hogs advantageously and satisfactorily, and how to produce milk and cheese and butter in quantities such as were never before contemplated'. If we are to maintain the agricultural population that we now have in western Canada, we must, I believe, do one of two things: either produce a finer quality of what we are now producing, and more economically than it is now produced, or discover other ways and means of using these products, or other products which can be grown on the soil and in the climate of western Canada.
The first words I uttered in this house come back to me. They were said on the minister's estimates. I put it to myself at that time, and I put it to the committee: what would1 a business man do under similar circumstances? If he had a surplus production problem in respect of his plant, he would do one of two things. Either he would call in merchandizing specialists to show him ways and means of creating a consumer demand for what he was producing, and thereby enable him to get rid of his surplus, or he would go out and get the best scientific brains and ability that money could buy in order to show him how he could economically change his factory facilities to the production of some other commodity which he could produce economically and which would find a market. That is the history of every successful industrial institution on the north American continent.

We have a surplus of wheat. I am not concerned about the possibility that that surplus will last very long. Once the war is over it will melt like the proverbial snowball. But I believe that two, three or four years after this war is over we shall be confronted with a surplus situation; and rather than depend on our ability to get rid of wheat as such, I should like to think that this country is employing the best scientific brains and ability available to find other products which can be economically produced in western Canada, or other means or uses for the products which are now produced in such enormous quantities. I believe that the answer is to be found in the brains and the test tubes of our young scientists. But having made it my business, in common with certain other western members to canvass the situation with the national research council-and these excellent gentlemen are doing a mighty fine work in that institution-I am impressed by this consideration :	from the very fact that that
institution is located here in the heart of industrial Canada, it is pressed more with the problems of industrial eastern Canada than with the urgency or the necessity of scientific research to find means of processing and making from our agricultural and other primary resources, new products and discovering or devising new uses for our agricultural and other natural products.
I hope that as a result of what has been said in the last few days under this particular item, the government-I have no doubt as to what the minister feels about it-will accede to the request of the agricultural representatives and see to it that, either under the Minister of Agriculture there are set up across this dominion laboratories manned by scientific men whose primary function shall be to discover new uses for our agricultural products, or else fresh emphasis shall be laid on that field of research with which our national research council is also charged. To my way of thinking the industrialists and manufacturers of eastern Canada, or of Canada as a whole if you will, are getting the benefit of the scientific brains and research work of the research council to a much greater extent than the primary producers. I do not say this has been to the detriment of those producers, but I do say the needs of industry are being over-emphasized as compared to the needs of our producers, who themselves individually are not impressed by the need for scientific research and study in the same way or to the same extent that the big manufacturing institutions of this dominion are.
I for one would be very much disappointed if something did not come out of this discussion which has been deliberately precipitated by thoughtful members of this house on both sides, who have no selfish motives or ideas but are trying to further the welfare of the country as a whole. At least that is my purpose, and I give the same credit to other hon. members who have spoken on this subject. Naturally I think of my own province, which is perhaps the only province in Canada which has a surplus of electrical energy, to say nothing of the coal and oil potentials with which to manufacture and process the natural products of the prairies. I look to the minister, as I am sure all agriculturists of western Canada look to him, as our champion, to find new ways and methods of using our products. I believe this will have to be done, and I think the answer will be found in the test tube and the scientifically trained men. I trust that never again will this item1 be the small, picayune thing it is now, in dollars and cents, having regard to the magnitude of the problem with which we are and shall be confronted in western Canada.

This question of surplus foods is no new thing; it is a very old question. Of course as the minister said-and I like to think of the Minister of Agriculture as having one of the hardest heads in Canada -if we look at this question from the point of view of the war, then we may take one attitude towards it; but if we take the long view as to what is to be our policy after the war is over, then that is something entirely different.
Hon. members have said that the great problem is, to set scientists at work to find the most scientific methods of spoiling as much human food as possible-that is what it amounts to-because we have or will have a so-called surplus. In the interval between the two wars there were millions of people all over the world who were underfed and undernourished. I believe it has been stated by the chief government medical health officr in Great Britain that over fifty per cent of the people of that country are underfed and undernourished, and I am- perfectly certain that Britain's record is not worse than that of any other country. I have not the figures; I cannot carry them in my head anyway, but I believe the situation is even worse in the United States. Yet when people were literally starving, farmers actually were being paid not to raise hogs, to plough up their potatoes, and to do all sorts of absurd things. Now we are told that the solution

is in the test tube. Well, as I have said before in this house, I have had a lifetime of experience in farming. I speak as a farmer, for the farmer, and I do not take a back seat to anyone in this house on that count. I have also had some preliminary training in chemistry, so that I know when people are talking a little science and when they are talking bunk. Most of it to-day is bunk; there is plenty of that.
What have we to do? I am not speaking of the war; for that is a totally different thing. War is hell, and just now we have to endure hell. I am speaking of the long-range programme, after the war is over, when surely we shall have a happier world, which means a better-fed world. Why has it been possible in the past to raise the food but impossible to distribute it? It is not a question of production but one of distribution, and in that connection you have to look not in the test tubes but in the ledgers of the bankers. Personally I have very little faith in so-called scientists; I think we need more hard-headed, common, horse sense. I think first the world has to learn-and people may laugh at it if they wish, but it is the truth and the war proves it-that under orthodox economics or orthodox finance or orthodox business or the orthodox price system it is impossible for the producer to distribute enough money to sell what he produces. That is why the consumer must be financed directly. If that were done the farmer would have no fear of not finding a ready market for everything he could produce. It is not a question of demand; the demand is there. It stands to reason that if people are underfed and undernourished, there is a demand for food; but the fact is that this demand is not effective because there is not enough money distributed to make it effective. So that rather than confess to ourselves that we have been blind in the past; rather than admit any mistakes on our part, the only solution we can see is to put our so-called scientists to work in order to spoil food and render it unfit for human consumption. If I might make a plea on behalf of the farmer-and I speak at present for the farmers as well as the rest of the people of Canada-it would be that we would put some real economists to work on the problem, so that in the end we could make financially possible anything -that is physically possible. We have done that during the war, and the only reason"we have done it is that in war time the canons of sound finance are silenced by the cannons of the enemy.

So far as potatoes are concerned, I have hesitated to raise the question here, but it seems that I cannot avoid it when a question is put to me direct. I understand that about 100 carloads of potatoes were shipped from Saskatchewan to the east during this period of comparative shortage, but I have been somewhat concerned ever since the war started about directing people to do things during war time, which they can do to advantage but which would probably put completely out

I do not know that our people in the west are particularly anxious to get into the growing of potatoes. In answer to the hon. member's first question, I think if we had the money to conduct the tests, and the men to conduct them, we could have had nearly all Canada as a restricted area at this time. That is, that would be the case if we were to take into consideration what the public want us to do. We have applications from all parts of Canada, and they come in, in as great or perhaps greater numbers from the west than from any other part. Since the war started we have been holding down our expenditures for this purpose. In the first place, we have been setting aside enough money to complete the inspection, and then re-inspect to be sure that the district is pretty well relieved of T.B. cattle. In addition to that, we have the condition that two or three counties may already be in, or two or three municipalities, and there would be a natural land division-a river, a lake or something of that kind forming the boundary-which would render a municipality part of that natural group, and where cattle would naturally move, as has been indicated by the hon. member for Acadia. We have attempted to overcome that situation by getting all that area in as soon as possible, and we have been carrying on tests in areas of that kind, even since we have been short of the cash required to do it to the extent we would desire to do it.
In addition to that, we are taking into consideration all of the requests made to us from different parts of Canada, and we are having those lined up so that we may deal with them as soon as we have the funds. The work is going on as rapidly as possible.

May I say to the hon. member for Acadia who has said that he does not see how these areas are supervised to keep out untested stock from other areas, that a review of the experience in the area in which I have lived since this work was undertaken discloses that strict provision is made against moving live stock which has not been tested into that area. No railway company or licensed trucker will take stock out of a stockyard and bring it into those areas without first advising the officials that it is being brought in. There might have been some transgression in respect of border-line stock sold at auction sales, or cattle running at large. But that is about all; and that is one of the reasons why the

Department of Agriculture has since attempted to establish natural boundaries, so that there might not be this transgression back and forth.
I should like to refer to another matter, *which came up in the agriculture committee this morning-Bang's disease. Several representations have been made of recent date to the minister urging that more work be done in connection with this disease which is causing considerable damage to certain herds in the country. It may cause greater loss to the individual than even bovine tuberculosis, and yet no provision is made for compensation. I have in mind two or three herds which, on account of their being afflicted with this disease, have proved almost a complete loss as far as usefulness and production are concerned. This is one branch of animal diseases which I feel should receive additional consideration. Its prevalence seems to be increasing, and something in a national way should be undertaken in an attempt to control it. Who stands the expense of the blood-tests for Bang's disease which must be made of cattle exported to the United States for breeding purposes?

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN PLACEMENT OP CARS
speechtext:
We bear the cost of inspecting cattle for Bang's which are going to the United States. This disease has been under consideration since long before I came to Ottawa, and it is still under consideration by the department. One of the first delegations I received after I came east was of live stock breeders from the eastern provinces, particularly Ontario, who had strong objections to the restrictions which were being imposed in connection with Bang's disease. The government had been advised to brand the diseased animal with a large "B", where everyone could see it. This would act as a warning to people that the animal had Bang's disease. As I say, strong objection was taken to this, and we compromised to the extent of branding only with a small "B" in the ear. Anyone could see this if they were looking for it, but it would not stare him in the face when he walked into a stable.
I cite this to indicate the objections that were made; these were similar to those made in the early days in connection with the tests for tuberculosis. A great many people who owned and bred cattle took strong exception to the tuberculosis test at one time, but this has been overcome by the people learning to appreciate what it means. The same thing happened in connection with Bang's; the people would not accept the tests as being final. Some contended that the disease could be cured, and we have been conducting investigations and making surveys with regard to the matter. We keep a check on cattle that are moving. We
 "
have to test cattle which enter the United States for breeding purposes, and they are not permitted to enter until a certificate has been issued. I have no doubt that in due course a method of dealing with this disease will be established, somewhat similar to that used, in connection with tuberculosis. I doubt very much, however, if we would be able to embark on a policy of that kind during the war period.

speechtext:
I would point out to the minister that there is a close relationship between diseases of animals and some that are transmitted from animals to human beings. The treatment of Bang's disease, for example, has been discussed here this afternoon. Bang's disease transmits to human beings what is known as undulant fever, for which no successful treatment has yet been discovered. Almost invariably that disease in human beings has a fatal termination. So that I would urge upon the minister that every possible avenue be explored for the eradication of Bang's disease and that animals having the disease be treated or slaughtered, for the protection of human life.
With reference to those animals which are treated for tuberculosis, the Department of Agriculture, in its health of animals branch, does not in my opinion go far enough. It should promote the pasteurization of milk throughout the whole country, even if it is necessary to subsidize certain provinces. The results of pasteurization in those provinces where it is in effect, particularly in Ontario, have been outstanding, especially with reference to bovine tuberculosis and milk-borne diseases transmitted to human beings such as typhoid and typhus fevers. I suggest to the minister that in view of this knowledge the department is not going far enough, and that it should encourage pasteurization in all the provinces, even going to the extent of subsidizing those provinces which are not in a position to carry it into effect.
I wish to say a word in reference to an epidemic that occurred two or three years ago among horses, particularly in Manitoba. There was an epidemic there of encephalitis
and poliomyelitis. These diseases were transmitted from horses to human beings. That was clearly established by investigations made by the department of health of Manitoba, with the valuable assistance of the Rockefeller Institute of New York. It was shown that there was a direct relationship between the disease which affected horses in certain areas of that province and the disease transferred to human beings. Are investigations being conducted with a view to eradicating these diseases and to develop other preventive measures for the protection of the health of human beings from animal diseases?

I do not wish to delay the passage of this item, but I should like to bring before the committee a matter which can be discussed1 on this item, or perhaps on a subsequent item. I wish to bring to the attention of the committee, the minister and the government information I have recently received from my part of the country indicating the state of mind of our farmers relating to marketing which I believe should receive our attention now instead of waiting to deal with it until after the war.
I agree with the leader of the opposition that our main objective is to supply food for our armed forces and for our allies. Hon. members will note, first, that the province of Alberta is now leading all Canada in the production of hogs, having passed the province of Ontario. Saskatchewan and Manitoba are also making tremendous strides in the production of hogs and cattle.
Those who have lived for many years in the west remember well what happened after the last war. I am sorry to have to go back so far to make my point, but it will be remembered that in 1919, the year following the end of the war, we had out west one of the hardest, longest and most costly winters we ever had, not even barring last winter, and that was particularly true of the northern parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta. It will also be remembered that at that time prices of hogs and cattle, in common with prices for everything else during the last war, were inflated, as
Supply-Agriculture

well as the prices of everything the farmers had to buy. An ordinary steer in the fall of 1919 would bring as high as S125.
That year, 1919, the winter set in early in the fall. I am mentioning this to show what the farmers have in mind, and I want to take back with me from this parliament and this government the assurance that the conditons which obtained at that time shall not be allowed to return. Winter set in on the 9th of October. It was twenty-five degrees below zero on the 10th of October. The weather broke a little in December, but snow remained on the ground until the latter part of April. If I remind the committee of the severity of that winter, it is to bring out the point that the cost of carrying our stock that winter was very great. I remember hay and fodder selling for as high as $75 a ton-. The farmers in my part of the country drove from 75 to 150 miles to haul in poor feed at terrific prices; but in spite of all their efforts, by the time February came, the municipalities and the government had to come to their assistance. The provincial government backed the notes of the municipal districts; the municipal districts accepted the notes of the farmers, and feed was obtained, but the result was that owners of stock went heavily in debt.
When the summer of 1920 came, that stock which could have been sold in the fall of 1919 for as high as $175 a head for a beef cattle and $140 for an ordinary steer, hogs for $17 a hundred pounds, with other prices in comparison, had to be sold for almost nothing. The market broke; the bottom dropped out of the market, and many of these steers and this stock which would have brought good prices in the previous fall died or had to be shot. It was a lamentable situation for which I blame no one, but I want hon. gentlemen to bear it in mind so that they will understand what is in the farmer's mind as to conditions that may obtain after this war unless something is done to prevent this. At that time cows went for $30 and hogs for S2.50 a hundred pounds. It was the most terrific crash in the west, not even barring that in 1931 and 1932. That is when most of our farmers went broke, through no fault of their own. They were not to blame for it, but somebody was to blame. The governments of this countiy and of the rest of the world were to blame for not being prepared to absorb the deflation which they must have known was bound to come after prices had risen so high. That is what I wish to bring before the committee.
I do not often speak in this house, and on this occasion I want to pay a tribute to one whom I consider to be the best Minister of

Agriculture this country has ever had. We have had first-class men as ministers of agriculture, but I think our own "Jimmie Gardiner", as we call him in the west, is the best of them all. From his knowledge of agriculture, his knowledge of the soil and of marketing conditions, his courage and ability, we are fortunate that in this crisis we have a man of his courage and ability to take charge of this great department. Those of us who have attended the sittings of the agriculture committee have come to realize his great ability, and the efficiency of the men with whom he has surrounded himself. Some of them were perhaps in the department before he was; I do not know; but one thing I will vouch for is that in every branch of his department, poultry, live stock, seed, farm administration, every official of the Department of Agriculture who appeared before us was competent in his field, and we heard and learned much. I wish to compliment these men upon the magnificent work they are doing. Canada is being extremely well served by the officials of the Department of Agriculture during this war.
What will be the situation after the war? I for one feel there is no danger. But the farmers are not satisfied with a letter from me or from anyone else. The French say "chat echaude craint l'eau froide,"-"the scalded cat is afraid of cold water". The terrific beating we took after the last war will never be forgotten by the present generation, and it is of no use telling the farmers that to-day we have very able men in charge of public affairs, men such as Churchill and Roosevelt, who framed the Atlantic charter to provide that there shall be freedom of marketing in this world after the war. The men we have in Canada, our Prime Minister, our Minister of Agriculture, and other ministers, are to me a guarantee that the condition that obtained after the last war will not obtain at the conclusion of the present hostilities. Unfortunately, however, we shall have to give the farmers some greater assurance than that. Recently I wrote a letter to the people in my constituency of Athabaska drawing their attention to the meeting that had been held at Hot Springs in which forty-four nations took part, along the lines of the Atlantic charter, for exactly the purpose that I have mentioned, namely, that provision will be made for the flow of goods after the war, for the distribution of foodstuffs, so that where there is a surplus in any country it will find its way to some other country that is in need of such goods. I hope it will be possible for the minister to arrange for a longer contract for hogs with

Supply-Agriculture
Great Britain. Whether it is possible I do not know, but I wish it could be extended for three years at least, because I think we should be in a position to assure our farmers and live stock men that there will be stability for that length of time.
I would remind the committee that to-day the west is the greatest producer of live stock, not barring Ontario, which for many years was the banner province in this line. I repeat, that some assurance will have to be given our farmers, if we cannot make a long-term contract for bacon, for instance, that they will be allowed gradually to cut down on their vast production, so that, if we are overproducing, the shock of that overproduction will be absorbed gradually from year to year.
Let me remind the business men in this house who are personally not interested in agriculture, as I am, and as so many other hon. members here are, that there is a tremendous investment in live stock in Canada. An hon. member from one of our cities was in conversation with me the other day on this matter, and he remarked to me that anyone can look after hogs. I was telling him of the shortage in help for looking after hogs and cattle in Canada, and that was the remark he made. What a mistaken idea! To-day, in order to raise hogs successfully, the kind of hogs which we want to sell to Britain, it takes first-class ability. If I may use the term, it is a profession. It is not something that is merely haphazard. It does not consist in taking a swillpail and throwing it at the hogs. Not at all; the work of feeding live stock and hogs is a matter for experts, and it entails a vast amount of labour. Therefore I appeal to the house and the country to do whatever is necessary to help our farmers before the war is over. The war may end suddenly, and the farmers are afraid of the consequences.

They laugh as long as you do not propose some crack-pot theory for the farmers of Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba, whereby people are supposed to live for nothing, to get something out of the air, or some kind of policy which will permit them to keep on howling without 72537-273
working. They howl at Ontario and Quebec; they howl at everyone; they laugh when someone propounds something that is in the interests of the farming community of the west.
However, to come back to what I was saying, the farmers believe that the war may end suddenly, and if the war does end suddenly they are afraid that their markets will be gone. A survey recently taken by a farming association in the northern part of Alberta brought surprising results. Seven farmers out of ten expressed the view that if the war were to end suddenly, or to end sooner than we anticipate, or whenever it does end, they will go out of the hog or cattle business immediately. That is a mistaken idea. I realize that we must do something to prevent that. As has been explained, we have recaptured the British market. We have supplied them with the goods which they require during the war, and so we have taken back the market which we lost after the last war on account of the quality of the goods which this country allowed to be shipped to that market. It took us twenty years to restore the Englishman's trust in us in that regard. We may have fooled the people there once, but you do not fool them for very long. We fooled them once after the last war, and the government of that day was to blame for allowing to be shipped to the English market bacon of a quality that was not fit for use. As I say, we have won that market back, and we have won it with first-class goods. That is why to-day we have a rigid inspection and are keeping to the grades we have established. This is something that is of interest to those who desire to work for a living and who do not dream of an imaginary world in which everything will come to everybody without doing anything to get it. I am sure that what I am saying will appeal to those who realize that the world will be the sort of world we make by hard labour and strict attention to business.
The farmers are looking to the government for one thing and one thing only, namely, a guarantee that this market will be kept intact for them; and if, as a result of conditions that may obtain in the world, it is necessary for us to reduce our herds of live stock, I trust that this will be done in an orderly manner so as to avoid any market crash, because there are very large investments which the farmers have made in this great business. Remember that Alberta has but a small percentage of the number of farmers in Ontario, and when you come to such a province and have to market more hogs than the great province of Ontario, you will realize the extent of the work which those men have to

do. You will realize that the men and women, the girls and boys are all helping in this business. They are willing to work overtime. They are not afraid of labour. They are satisfied with the price they are getting at present. They understand the conditions, but they want an assurance that their great investment in buildings and herds, in first-class animals, pure-bred stock, shall not be allowed to be destroyed' for want of a policy.
I say, therefore, that it may become the duty of this parliament to take action to ensure this. I for one hope and believe that there will be orderly marketing after the war and that Britain, the United States, Canada and Russia and many other countries will enter into agreements for that orderly marketing of our surplus. I have no fears so far as our surplus wheat is concerned, but there may be some months, a season or two, when some disorganization is bound to happen. That being the case, I personally believe that we should have a floor under the price of our stock so that the farmer can carry on, knowing that he will have a fair return, until the four freedoms have been established and world markets have been opened to him, so that he can sell his hogs and other live stock for the things needed at home. It may take a year or two. No one imagines that the affairs of the world will be settled in twenty-four hours after the war. No one imagines that the new order is something in the form of a blueprint to be laid on the table so that one can point to' it and say to the people, "There is your road, follow it." Long negotiations may take place, and during that time there will be need of some stability. .
I hope that at some time in the next twelve months we shall wake up one fine morning and be called upon to wave our flags to celebrate the victory of the allied nations. When that time arrives, Mr. Chairman, I want to have this matter before the house, so that we shall act all together apart from any party politics, if it is necessary to support our farmers, who have made such sacrifices during this war, working the longest hours of anybody. Next after those men who are flying to-night over Germany and Italy, next to the sacrifices and the hardships endured by those boys and by those who are travelling the ocean to-night looking for the lurking beasts of prey under the waves, and all the others in all the armed forces, the men working harder are the farmers of this country, who, though short of help and in spite of great difficulties, are doing a tremendous job.

I realize that I have taken more of the committee's time than I wanted to, but I am speaking of something which I have much at heart and something which I know appeals to every hon. member, in appealing for this class which is doing so well for us during the war, the farmers, the farmers' boys, the farm women and girls. It is on behalf of these farmers I make my plea to our farmer Minister of Agriculture, a man whom I know has so deeply at heart the welfare of the people on the farms, whose heart is with the farmers of the west, where his own farm is situated, and where he has lived and worked so long on behalf' of the agriculturists. To his department and to this committee I appeal. It may be necessary to place a floor under the price of our live stock, so that our farmers will be assured of a reasonable return and will be able to reduce their herds if this should be necessary, without suffering the terrific losses and hardships of 1919 to 1921.

week the committee on rehabilitation agreed to recommend to the house that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act be applied to all Canada. Being somewhat of an enthusiast about rehabilitation work, I should like to see that done, but I do not know that it would be possible to carry it out at the preseut stage of the war. I would hope that some day the benefits which have been given to parts of three provinces might be passed on to other people in Canada. One argument for the delaying of this action is the fact that many of our men will be coming back from overseas, and much of the work which would have to be done under legislation of
this kind could be done then to good advantage. It would provide employment for men, particularly those who have been associated with engineering and other activities of that kind that go with war.
On the other hand, in Saskatchewan-it goes under another name in Alberta and also in New Brunswick-we have the northern areas plan which the hon. member for North Battleford will be quite familiar with. This plan has to do with persons who were rather hurriedly moved from the drouth areas into the northern district. Some of them were placed on bush land which cost $40 an acre to clear. Under this plan assistance was given in clearing up the land. The province of Quebec carries out a plan without any assistance from the dominion government, under which plan the same work is carried on and has been for some years. When settlers are moved into newer areas the province provides equipment similar to that used on the Alaska highway, but not quite so heavy, to clear the land and level it off so that the settler may have something to start with. This work is most beneficial and helpful to people who live in areas of that kind. It has been carried on for several years in Saskatchewan. My understanding is that most of the people who W'ere on relief at the time the plan was started are now able to carry on for themselves. The plan is still being carried on by the province without any assistance, but to a 'esser extent than it was earlier.
The way we have worked under this act is to define roughly the drouth areas. We found by experience that there was only one practical way to do this, namely, to take the river basins. We have not been able to stop short of the height of land at the northern side. Recently we drew a line from some place north of Prince Albert along the northern row of sections up to the height of land north of the North Saskatchewan river to the divide where the water goes north or comes south. I do not know whether this went into the hon. member's constituency. We followed the height of land until we reached the Alberta boundary, where we went along the height of land marking the Battle river basin and others southward to the United States boundary. In Manitoba we follow the height of land forming the boundary of the Assiniboine river basin. We follow the height of land right down to north of Winnipeg. All inside that triangle is called the drouth area and is covered by the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I cannot say at the moment that it will be possible in the immediate future to extend it, but I

After chatting with some of the officials I was hoping that we might see a little increase in this vote this year, but I suppose we should be grateful that we are getting enough to carry on during war time. I would be ready to support such an increase in order to permit the construction under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act of some badly needed pastures and stock-watering projects in our part of the country. This would permit the increased stock raising required in connection with our war effort.
When speaking in this chamber on another occasion I mentioned the benefits to Canada as a whole, and more especially to the west, which had been obtained from this act which was passed by the Bennett administration and greatly extended by the present government under the able administration of the Minister of Agriculture. When the Hon. George Spence appeared before the reconstruction committee and said what had been accomplished up to date at that time and could further be done, it was considered to be the most constructive paper given before the sittings of that good committee. He said that of the 3,000,000 acres of poor land broken during the first world war which should not have been broken, one and a quarter million acres are now included in sixty-seven community pastures, which during last season had taken care of over 65,000 head of stock. These pastures are not yet up to capacity. They are managed locally and nearly all are beginning to pay their way. Some have a small sinking fund put away for repairs and rebuilding at a later time.
Plans are also in the hands of the engineers to convert another one and a half million acres into seventy-three more of these pastures which are badly needed. Many head of stock are now turned away since the pastures are getting pretty well filled with stock by farmers adjoining the present pastures. Those from a distance cannot get their stock into these pastures. More than 20,000 small stockwatering projects have been completed, assisted by engineering advice and by payment of part of the cost under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, and there are many more applications for such funds.
Many of these dug-outs have been so constructed as to irrigate gardens during the dry season. I may say that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has assisted with several small irrigation projects where fruit, vegetables and fodder are very successfully grown in dry

seasons, and there are more applications for these works which are held up for the duration of the war.
When the war is won, Mr. Chairman, I would be bold enough to suggest that the name of this act be changed to the Canadian Farm Rehabilitation Act, an act to serve all Canada; to assist in the draining of swamp lands in the maritime provinces and rehabilitate Ontario and Quebec farms and the Kamouraska cut-over lands, and rehabilitate burnt-over timber land. I am sure, Mr. Chairman, the people of the west are prepared to cooperate in this and other work of this kind. But to rehabilitate western Canada we must have water, which has been referred to' by the Hon. George Spence as "liquid gold on the prairies".
Several years ago we formed in our community the Saskatchewan-Alberta Irrigation Association along the border of the two provinces, and gave a great deal of study to this matter. On one occasion I took a surveyor and engineer, a Mr. Campbell, on an extended trip at our own expense to the eastern irrigation project in Alberta, where we counselled with Mr. Gray, who was the manager, and with his engineers who had made such an outstanding success of their project.
We secured a great deal of valuable information generally and also with regard to the much talked of "William Pearce, North Saskatchewan river stock watering scheme" which, of course, is much different from what we saw at Brooks, for Brooks is strictly an irrigation project. They can and do grow everything and operate a canning factory successfully. A wonderful good-sized town has grown up there and several small industries are flourishing. Some of the people from our part of Saskatchewan have moved in there, made their homes and are doing quite well.
We then proceeded with Mr. Campbell to Stettler to investigate storage possibilities at Buffalo lake and were well satisfied that there were huge storage possibilities both at Buffalo lake and Sullivan lake, at Hanna, Alberta, where 75,000 acres of land could be brought under irrigation. We then followed the natural flow of the water as set out by Mr. William Pearce himself in his papers. That is down Sounding creek, where the early settlers cut wood; thence down Eye Hill creek, entering Saskatchewan at Cosine, which is in the constituency that I have the honour to represent.
Eye Hill creek runs to Manitou lake, near Unity, where more storage could be provided.

Thence, with a little cutting you could bring water into Tramping lake, which is a very large lake, thirty miles in length and spoken of by Mr. Pearce and the P.F.R.A. engineers as having huge storage possibilities which would serve a large area in this district.
The engineers' reports point out that over 100.000 acres in the Kindersley, Glidden to Eston district can be irrigated and that three-quarters of a million acres in the Elrose, Rosetown to Saskatoon district could also be irrigated.
There are over 56,000.000 tons of snow water from mountains, Mr. Chairman, running away into lake Winnipeg and Hudson bay every day over and above what is being used for irrigation and power in Alberta. It would be a huge undertaking; but if these 56,000,000 tons of snow water which run away each day were stored-and there is storage-and then spread over our farms, if only a few acres on each farm, we would be doing more to rehabilitate western Canada than could be done in any other way that has been proposed to date. Instead of losing our people we would be able to make homes for more. While the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act has been and is doing good work, I should like to see this work extended and take in the Pearce plan at least. The Pearce plan could be gone ahead with at a reasonable cost of a few million dollars and would provide water for stock watering and for mixed farming. That would call for only a few million dollars to carry the water through the natural channels at a small cost per annum. But for further rehabilitation an expenditure of an additional, say eighty million dollars or, as the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) has suggested, 100 to 150 million dollars would supply water, storage, canals et cetera to irrigate about one and a half million acres and also provide power for secondary industries. We could grow fruits and vegetables, feed and fodder for stock, build homes and keep off relief.
Before closing, I desire to thank the hon. member for Davenport for what he has advocated in this house and on the public platforms in support of this expenditure and great undertaking for western Canada. He has been very fair and., Mr. Chairman, I am sincere when I say that with his knowledge and understanding he should be honoured with the degree of doctor.
I also desire to thank the minister and his P.F.R.A. officials for the information they have furnished to the Saskatchewan-Alberta Irrigation Association before war was declared, at which time we folded up our organization
for the duration, our splendid secretary, Mr. Galbraith joined the army. He is now serving his country overseas. But I more especially thank Major Duncan Stewart, K. C. of Calgary, for the assistance he has given me, which includes a letter from the late Senator Burns as well as papers and blueprint plans which belong to the estate of the late William Pearce, lent by Mr. Pearce's son. In his letter Senator Burns refers to himself as a converted old-timer. The letter is written to Colonel J. F. Dennis, formerly of the Canadian Pacific railway land department. I have received a good deal of valuable information from these papers.

This is an appropriation in which the eastern farmers are interested, more particularly those at the head of the bay of Fundy. The special committee on reconstruction and rehabilitation made a recommendation that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act should be enlarged to enable work to be done all over Canada. I believe this recommendation was made with special reference to the marsh lands at the head of the bay of Fundy. The committee took considerable evidence. The Hon. J. A. McDonald, Minister of Agriculture and Marketing of Nova Scotia, came and gave evidence before the committee. The minister of agriculture of New Brunswick was prepared to come and will probably still come. Resolutions have been passed unanimously by the legislatures of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, by boards of trade and other bodies asking that the federal government assume responsibility for the reclaiming of these marsh lands, so that they will not revert to floating bogs, because the drainage channels become blocked, or inundated by the sea, owing to breakage of dikes and aboideaux.
I know from statements of the minister that he is personally sympathetic with this proposal. I know that his deputy minister, Doctor Barton is sympathetic, and I know that the director of experimental farms, Doctor Archibald, has for years shown his interest. Experiments ,have been carried on at the experimental station under Mr. Baird at Nap-pan, at the head of the bay of Fundy, showing the productivity of these lands when properly cultivated. Land that is not drained and cultivated will grow only half a ton of the poorest class of hay, while land of the same character, within 100 feet, can be made to produce hay of the very best quality, yielding from three to four tons per acre.
Recently there has been great interest on the part of the marsh owners, who have appointed

Supply-Agriculture

representatives of march bodies, who are prepared to come to Ottawa as a delegation from the head of the bay of Fundy from New Brunswick, from my county, and the county represented by the Minister of Finance. This delegation is waiting for word as to when they may come to Ottawa in order to make representations, so that an appropriation may be made in order that work may be undertaken this year.
It is necessary that the work be commenced now if these lands are to be made available for farmers who come back after the war or are discharged from war industries, because it will take some years before the full benefits are derived.
There has been expended under this act up to 1942, a total of $14,547,875 for prairie farm rehabilitation, and quite an important part of that work is the control of water for the benefit of the farmers of the prairies. All those interested in agriculture in Canada are in sympathy with this. There was appropriated last year $2,000,000, and we are now dealing with a vote of $2,000,000 for the current year. We at the head of the bay of Fundy ask that this apply to our marshlands. I believe that the minister is in sympathy with the proposal, and I would ask that the appropriation be made available this year, or otherwise that an additional appropriation of at least a quarter of a million dollars be provided in order that the work may be started at once.
There are other special appropriations for the west, such as $500,000 under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, as voted last year; an appropriation of $28,175,000 to provide for wheat acreage reduction payments, and so on. There was also an appropriation last year of $1,950,000 to provide for assistance to encourage the improvement of cheese and cheese factories, and another appropriation of $50,000, totalling last year $32,675,000. Not one dollar of that was expended in eastern Canada. This year the estimates under the same headings total $8,390,000. Not one dollar of last year's vote and not a dollar this year is to be applied under this act to eastern Canada unless the minister adopts the recommendation of the committee and has this act extended or makes a special appropriation in order that work on the marshlands may be undertaken at once.
When the minister sets his heart upon a project such as this in the administration of his department he has usually been successful, and I believe the interest he has shown in previous years, and the interest he has now in this matter, will induce him before the
[Mr. P. C. Black.:
end of the session to arrange for an appropriation in order that work may be undertaken. It is proposed that the work be done mainly by machinery so as to reduce man-power requirements to the minimum. It is necessary that the main river outlets be opened up; that the drainage channels which have filled up with silt and vegetation be cleaned out; that machinery be provided which can be used for opening the smaller drainage ditches, and that the dikes and aboideaux that have gone down or weakened in recent years be restored.
The departments of agriculture in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are, I believe, prepared to make some contribution toward this work. These marsh lands are the most fertile lands in all Canada. They attracted our early settlers, and if they are not reclaimed, agriculture as we have known it in that part of Canada might as well be abandoned, as the production from these lands is used to build up the fertility of farm uplands which should carry a hundred head of stock where now there is hardly one. One acre of marshland properly cultivated involves the cultivation of five acres of upland. The production of live stock, fat cattle, and dairy products would reestablish agriculture as it was in former years, and, I believe, to an even greater extent.
I am appreciative of the attitude of the Minister of Agriculture in previous years with respect to this proposal. I believe that he is as sympathetic as ever, and it is the opinion of farmers in eastern Canada that, if he is really determined, an appropriation will be made available this year.
I do not wish to take my seat without expressing my appreciation on behalf of eastern Canada and especially on behalf of the marsh owners of the sympathetic consideration which has been given to .this proposal by all the members of the committee, including those from western Canada, who have benefited by these large expenditures, by hon. members on the committee from central Canada, and by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Henderson) who preceded me this evening. I make this appeal to the minister, to the government and to the members of this committee that an appropriation be made available this year, so that some work will be undertaken to reclaim these fertile marsh lands at the head of the bay of Fundy.
