The proposal that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act be changed to constitute it a Canada Farm Rehabilitation Act commends itself to me. I have felt ever since I came to this chamber that Canada must be looked upon as one great united economy. Anything that injures any part of it injures every part, and conversely, anything that helps any part helps all Canada. I believe that a sympathetic ear should be lent to the voice of a representative from any part of this dominion, and I believe that the appropriation for this kind of work should be greatly increased. I have contended that now for some years.
I should like to mention to the minister one project which vitally concerns my particular constituency, the project known as the Lethbridge southeast water conservation project. Members of the committee perhaps will have had it brought to their attention in times past. Down in the southwestern corner of Alberta there are two rivers known as the St. Marys river and the Milk river. Both of these rivers are international; that is, they flow on each side of the border. The waters have been divided between Canada and the United 72537-274J
States, but so far Canada has failed to use the portion of water which was allotted to her. It is well that members of the committee should have in mind that it is a well understood principle that in cases like this, where the interests of two nations are concerned, if one nation fails to use to advantage its share of water there is a likelihood that it will lose its right to that water, and the nation which has been using its share to advantage will have a claim on the water which is not being used by the other nation. If this principle were applied in the case to which I refer, Canada would lose very heavily and lose for all time.
The Lethbridge southeast water conservation project has been examined time and again. Recommendations were made as far back as 1921, and before, that something concrete and definite should be done, and done without further delay. But after the last war the whole matter was allowed to rest, because the governments in power said, "We have not the money; we must retrench now and pay for the war." The result was that for a generation this project was allowed to remain neglected. Now if history is to repeat itself we are likely to find a similar thing. It is an easy enough matter for us to rise in our places in this chamber and assert that as soon as this war is over, somehow or another there will be a boundless amount of money, now going to the war, available for use in rehabilitation. Unless the system under which we are working changes, no such thing as that will happen; as soon as the war is over we shall have hon. members rising in this house and contending that we must retrench and tighten our belts and pay for the war. The result will likely be that all of these projects will simply become day-dreams.
I just want to draw the attention of the minister, as emphatically as I can in a short time, the need for looking after the Lethbridge southeast water conservation project. The minister understands this well; he has been over the ground, and I believe he has shown great sympathy in the matter, but is restrained largely by financial consideration from taking action. I have contended privately before the minister and in public that I do not believe financial considerations should be allowed to interefere with the development of this project. Only $15,000,000 are involved, and 345,000 acres of the finest land in the Dominion of Canada would be brought under irrigation as a result of the development of that project.
If the findings of the international food committee mean anything more than the paper they are written on; if they really do mean that we are going to need a lot of food after the war, and we are going to use the food for
Supply-Agriculture

the benefit of the people, obviously the food producing areas of this country should be developed to a high degree. There should therefore be no justification for delay in the matter of constructing the key dams and reservoirs of this great project. Four million dollars would be sufficient to build the main reservoir, which is known as the St. Marys reservoir, situated near Spring Coulee on St. Marys river in my constituency. It would take probably two or three years to build that reservoir even if we commenced in 1943. I contend that we should commence in 1943, not just to investigate and look over the ground and dream of what we are going to do, but should do something in 1943.
There is one other aspect of the question which is quite serious and which is becoming more urgent all the time. They are having dry weather in my constituency in southern Alberta and, as the hon. member for Medicine Hat pointed out this evening, they are having dry weather in his constituency as well. When dry weather comes in these constituencies it is an exceedingly serious matter. The present facilities for supplying water to the land now under irrigation in four major irrigation projects in my constituency are not sufficient. The water needed in times of stress, such as we are passing through now, would be available if the St. Mary's reservoir were constructed, and I think it only fair and just to the people in that area that they should be provided with ample water in time of need. This constitutes another very strong reason for proceeding at the earliest possible moment with the construction of reservoirs in connection with this water conservation project.

This item calls for the expenditure of $2,000,000; this year there is neither an increase or a decrease. Reference has been made to the fact that the government may consider the suggestion made by the reconstruction committee that the provisions of this act be extended to all Canada, and some hon. members have expressed themselves as being favourable to that step. I have been wondering what the minister's idea is in that regard, and if he really means to give that suggestion favourable consideration. Personally I would not be very anxious to see this act extended to the whole of Canada, because I see the possibility that it might become a racket.
When this act was passed in 1934-I believe this is the eighth year it has been in operation -it was intended to assist the farmers in certain areas in western Canada where there had been drouth for four or five years. The situation in certain parts of Saskatchewan was very serious, and this act was intended to

rehabilitate those areas. It also outlined certain principles. The act was designed to assist farmers to conserve moisture, to store water and to work out schemes for the better utilization of land. The main purposes for which the act was passed were good. A great deal has been done by the present government, and I give credit to. the minister for being most anxious to carry on the projects that were commenced and to support the principles outlined in this measure, but I think in some instances these projects have been developed to a very much greater extent than was ever intended.
Before we are finished with this item I hope the minister will* give us a great deal more information with respect to water storage schemes, pastures that have been established and particularly some of the dam projects. To give the committee some idea of what might happen, I asked for a return in February and another in March to show the costs of certain projects being carried on in the Qu'Appelle valley which, I may say, is the boundary between the constituencies of the Minister of Agriculture and myself, so that these projects to which I have reference now might be called our projects. I find that certain surveys have been carried on in that valley during the last two years, on which some fifty-three people have been employed at a cost of something over $50,000. The returns also show that three dams are under construction, to cost approximately $127,000 on completion. But I do not think we are obtaining value for the money being expended on these dams. The one at Round lake flooded certain areas that were used by the Indians for haying purposes, and they have practically lost the entire use of that land. I should like the mnister to tell the committee if those Indans were reimbursed for the damage done and the loss sustained, and what agreement was reached with the Indian affairs branch or the men on the reserve in that connection. I have looked over that situation, and considerable loss has been occasioned.
Perhaps the minister would give a more or less detailed statement in connection with this work, because it is of interest not only to me but to other hon. members from the northern part of Saskatchewan, who know something of what the building of these dams has meant. No doubt the minister has a copy of this return, so that I need not read the questions I asked and the information that was given, but I should like a little further information which he might supply at a later date. I would ask the minister to be good enough to give me the home addresses of the fifty-three men employed in these survey parties.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN PLACEMENT OP CARS
speechtext:
Were any of the dams
washed out this year on account of the extra flow of water?

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN PLACEMENT OP CARS
speechtext:
There was one at Willows on Lake of the Rivers in Saskatchewan. We have had trouble with this one on two different occasions. I have been down to look at it personally. We may have to abandon it, but we have attempted to store water there. With the amount of water there was in the streams this year w-e have been surprised that we have not lost more dams.
We have fifty-seven pastures operating and ten under construction. I may say that so far as these pastures go, the treasury is not concerned after they are once constructed. The capital cost is put up by the treasury and that will stand for some twenty years at least. The posts that are used are creosoted and should be good for that length of time. Fees are paid by the farmers who put cattle or horses into the pasture, and these are more than sufficient to pay the cost of operation since , there is a surplus of $38,215.01. In this connection, we have three ideas in mind. First, there is the community pasture where the farmers around the pasture are organized. They have their own association which controls the number of cattle that may be put on the pasture by each farmer and also it takes care of the fees. We appoint a manager who becomes a secretary of the association. As I have just pointed out, the fees are more than sufficient to pay the operating costs including the salaries of the managers.
In addition to that, we have the reserve pastures that I spoke of before the dinner hour. These are large areas, some hundred thousand acres in extent. We have fenced them to keep out stock in the good years and they will be available in drouth years. They grew grass as abundantly as before live stock ran over the country at all. Conditions in that section of the province are such that, with water provided, much of the live stock can run out through the winter. Then there is another form of pasture which is associated with an irrigated area. This is a community pasture in which lands are irrigated outside the pasture and produce the fodder and grain for the live stock which runs on the pasture in the summer time. AH these have been operating successfully, and I do not think the neighbourhood would like to be without them in the future.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN PLACEMENT OP CARS
speechtext: Is there not some way in which the payment of the bonus to the widow can be expedited? There are cases where payment has been held up for a couple of years until the man's estate is settled. I spoke of this a year ago, and the minister said then that an amendment would be introduced whereby it would be possible to pay a bonus to the widow immediately if she were in necessitous circumstances.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN PLACEMENT OP CARS
speechtext: We had no authority under the regulations as they were to make a payment to the beneficiary of the estate when the person who had a claim had died, but we did go ahead and make some payments after considerable difficulty. But a change has been made in the regulations within the past three or four weeks which now makes it possible for us to make the payment automatically.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN PLACEMENT OP CARS
speechtext:
There is another matter to which I wish to refer. Subsection 5 of section 8 of the regulations reads:
8. No person shall be considered to be a farmer under the act unless:
5. If residing with a parent or a brother, he is of the full age of twenty years and operates the farm as a separate unit, and the farm consists of at least a quarter-section of land.
I can understand the need for such a provision in the regulations to prevent a large farmer from dividing his farm up among his children in order to benefit by a larger bonus payment, but here is the case of a son living with his father in a town. The father is not a farmer himself but rents his farm to his son, who farms it and makes a good job of it. That boy should be granted the bonus; but he has been denied it on the ground that he is only nineteen years of age. It seems to me that we should try to encourage these young people rather than discourage them from carrying on that type of work. This is no case of the father trying to get a larger bonus because he is not farming at all; he is renting his farm to his son, and the son is denied the bonus on the ground that he is a minor living with his parents. I do not think the intention of the regulation was to deny that boy the bonus. The intention was to prevent a farmer from dividing up a large farm in order to get a larger bonus. The case to which I refer is that of Jack Turton of Consort, Alberta.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN PLACEMENT OP CARS
speechtext: There has been some difficulty. In this particular case he would be denied the bonus because he was living in the town and not on the farm.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN PLACEMENT OP CARS
speechtext:
No; he was denied it
because he was a minor.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN PLACEMENT OP CARS
speechtext:
There would be the two
reasons.

subtopic: ALLEGED DISCRIMINATION IN PLACEMENT OP CARS
speechtext:
No; I will read the letter from the superintendent, Department of Agriculture, Edmonton. He writes:
With regard to the above-mentioned claim, we wish to advise that owing to the fact that Jack Turton was not of the full age of twenty years when filing the_ cultivated acreage report, he cannot be considered for payment under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
There have been two other letters, and in none of the letters is the question raised of the young man's living in town. He is denied the bonus on the ground that he is a minor living with bis father. Perhaps I had better go into the matter further with the minister at some later time, but where there is no question of a father dividing up his farm among his children in order to get a larger bonus, when his son rents the farm from him and is making a good job of it, does not the minister agree he should be entitled to the bonus? Why deprive him of it just because he is nineteen years of age?
